items.content:
Microsoft has introduced Open AI's GPT-5.6 family of models into Microsoft 365 Copilot. In terms of business value, what that means is improved quality of what Copilot can produce and reducing the effort it takes you to get there. 

Knowledge work is complex - multistep, ambiguous, and spread across tools and files. With stronger reasoning for agentic, multi-step work, GPT-5.6 helps Copilot take on more of that complexity more efficiently, moving faster from initial ideas to more complete work.

These models are available in the main Copilot chat experience, as well as in Word, Excel, and PowerPoint. That means you can use it to reason through more complex asks, produce stronger drafts, clearer analysis and richer presentations.

For those who have been unable to work with Anthropic models (because of restrictions on offshore processing), this opens up some of the more advanced reasoning and complex use cases for Copilot in your environments.

I'll be testing this in my environment and in my everyday work to push the boundaries and see what's possible. Follow along for more, or share your experiences here.

article.title: Key Takeaways from Gartner Supply Chain Symposium 2026
article.subtitle: supplychainnow.com
article.linkLabel: Open article: Key Takeaways from Gartner Supply Chain Symposium 2026 by supplychainnow.com

items.content:
The world of supply chain management is full of "experts."

I'm concerned that in the Supply Chains to Admire work, we find that global multinationals struggle to scale performance. We are not able to achieve economies of scale. One reason is a lack of focus on supply chain fundamentals.

Many "experts", I find, dance in the aura of new shiny objects- pontificating on the promise of the autonomous supply chain and touting the power of agentics. "Faster horses?" I say, "Not so fast." Let's start with a clear definition of supply chain fundamentals — first-principles alignment, a redefinition of the company's relationship to data, and clarity on lead time — to ensure we don't make mistakes. 

I close this blog post by challenging companies to measure their supply chain entropy resulting from the lack of a clear definition of lead time.

Each week, I face a blank screen, my fingers reach for words, and slowly a blog appears. Developing the skills to become a writer has been an amazing and rewarding process.   

I never aspired to be a blogger. My first attempts were painful — my first blog, published on January 26th, 2010, took me a week to write. Over the past 14 years, I have published 612 blog posts.

Each week, I share research, case studies, and observations. The blog is independent. There is no advertising or third-party content. Just me, an old gal, trying to help supply chain leaders. My goal is to share unique insights for business innovators.

Today, I am proud that my blog, the Supply Chain Shaman, ranks as #11 of 100 supply chain blogs analyzed by Feedspot. 

So, next week, somewhere in the world, you will find me tapping on a keyboard. (My electronic keyboard never fits in my briefcase.) Writing the blog now brings me joy.

On my 72nd birthday, I want to thank you for being a reader. I hope that somewhere, I helped someone drive value in their supply chain.

I am proud to share that Unilever has been recognised by Gartner as a Supply Chain Master for the eighth consecutive year, alongside Amazon, Apple and P&G. 

I am even prouder of our team, and what this recognition represents: the supply chain excellence we are building and our continued transformation in line with business needs to be a stronger growth driver for Unilever, especially in today’s volatile world. 

Demand is moving faster. Consumers expect more choice, better availability and faster fulfilment. Inflation, cost pressure and geopolitical uncertainty continue to test resilience. In this reality, our supply chain has become a source of competitive advantage. 

We’re using AI and digital tools at scale to improve service, support faster decisions and reduce manual work. We are adapting our operations for shorter innovation cycles and faster-changing demand, from social-first commerce to more responsive product launches. We are also investing in our people and digital capability, while building more resilient and responsible value chains, including in areas such as palm oil. 

And we’re seeing results. We have shortened demand cycles from months to hours, concept-to-pilot timelines reduced to 12 weeks, more predictive customer operations, stronger digital capability across our teams, and value chains that are more transparent and resilient.  

Thank you to everyone across Unilever and our partner network.

items.content:
Today, I am proud to share the 2026 Supply Chains to Admire report. This report is based on public reporting by manufacturing and retail companies for the ten-year period of 2016-2025. 

Please join me in celebrating the success of these 32 top-performing companies. 

Before you start. A small warning. (This is not a light read. I share all of the calculations, orbit charts, and sector analysis in detail. As you read the report, I encourage you to reflect on the headwinds facing each industry. The demand challenges and market shifts abound.) 

In parallel, to help companies use the methodology, we are releasing the Dynamic Benchmarking product on AskLora.ai to enable companies to view metrics more holistically and understand their organizational, process, and technology maturity. 

The benchmarking is currently limited to the 450 companies in the Supply Chains to Admire report, but in July, the analysis will be for all public manufacturers and retailers and will enable the comparison of all companies--independent of size and region of public reporting-- to be compared against both the companies in the Gartner Top 25 dataset and the Supply Chains to Admire analysis.

I bet many of you have never seen an actual chipmunk (and weren't expecting one in your LinkedIn feed 😆). Here's one of Chip & Dale's cousins drinking out of a dog water bowl on my back porch, just outside my home studio window.

In fact, this bowl has served a wild variety of wildlife (that I've seen & probably plenty more that I haven't): plenty of birds and squirrels also stop in for a brief respite as temps begin to rise here in Georgia. There just might be a business lesson there, as great organizations create successful ecosystems where value spreads far beyond the original target.

Moving on from a moment of nature zen, let's get into a Tuesday Morning Rundown:

👉  Pizza Hut has been sold. A brand inseparable from my childhood has new owners: LongRange Capital. Also, Pizza Hut locations in China will be acquired by Yum China in a separate deal. As CNBC reports: "In the U.S., the pizza chain has transitioned from the sit-down format and salad bars of yore to focus on delivery and carryout — far behind the curve. Rival Domino’s Pizza has gobbled up market share from Pizza Hut for years; third-party delivery apps like DoorDash have further stolen sales from the chain."

👉  Netrio recently released research based on insights from 401 U.S. IT leaders at organizations with 200 to 5,000 employees. It "shows that AI has already moved well beyond experimentation in the mid-market. In total, 82% of respondents said AI is already in production somewhere in their organization or in widespread use, yet only 26% said AI is scaled and governed enterprise-wide, highlighting a gap between AI adoption and operational maturity." It found that the top barriers to scaling AI were "security, privacy and compliance (19%), data readiness (17%), integration complexity (16%), and lack of internal expertise (10%)." Link below.

👉  Speaking of intriguing research, come join us LIVE on June 23rd at 12 noon ET, where we host Lora Cecere on Supply Chain Now (along with special friends Dave Winstone & Wael ABDELMALEK). We'll dive into Supply Chains to Admire 2026 and "Ask Lora". You know it will be a No Fluff Zone!. See link below in comments.

👉  Uncertainty is still the flavor of the year: the USMCA renewal discussions are set to become an episode of "Days of Our Lives". Even if the U.S. truly doesn't plan to renew, the agreement essentially stays in place for 10 years...UNLESS the U.S. withdraws (which only requires 6 months notice). Buckle up folks.

👉  Check out our 1st two interviews from Gartner Supply Chain Symposium '26: Abdil Tunca with Gartner and Jeff Jackson with Penske Logistics. See playlist link below in comments.

👉  You know I love a good case study: our friends at EasyPost worked with a re-commerce marketplace to save $2M in shipping costs AND eliminate 273,000 late deliveries. All with no new carriers, no renegotiated contracts & no new headcount. See link in comments to learn more.

Have a wonderful week, folks.

One of the biggest shifts I’ve observed in manufacturing over the last few years is that optimizing a single metric is becoming increasingly dangerous.

Most leaders don’t tell me they want AI.

They tell me they want to:

* improve on-time delivery
* increase throughput
* reduce inventory
* improve utilization
* improve customer service

All valid objectives.

The challenge is that today’s operating environment is far more interconnected and uncertain than it used to be.

Improving one metric often comes at the expense of another.

I’ve seen manufacturers improve utilization while increasing lead times.

Reduce inventory while hurting service levels.

Increase throughput while creating downstream bottlenecks.

The real challenge is no longer optimizing a department, a process, or even a system.

It’s understanding the trade-offs across planning, operations, supply chain, quality, maintenance, and customer commitments—and making better decisions as conditions change.

In many ways, manufacturing is becoming less about optimization and more about continuous balancing.

The leaders who can navigate those trade-offs quickly will have a significant advantage over the next decade.

What trade-off is your organization struggling with most today?

items.content:
This study of Franklin Sports shines a light on the work that needs to be done at the sales account level to challenge a retail forecast, and also highlights the importance of a new technique for a forecast engine — reinforcement learning. 

Artificial intelligence comes in many forms — large language models, generative AI, machine learning, unstructured text mining, deep learning, neural networks, reinforcement learning, agents, and agentics. While the industry is wigging out about agentics, I think reinforcement learning is a great step forward in the journey of demand management, and the challenger forecast is a useful model to conceptualize the work happening at the sales account team level as they forecast sales.
